title: Cut it in half
hookLine: rules run too long: a man swears to keep the basics, no more and no less, and the Prophet answers
tomorrow: a young captive asked for a ten-day test. what was he testing?

lines: WHAT DOES ISLAM ASK OF ME?
HE SUCCEEDS, IF HE IS TRUTHFUL.
cards: First versions tend to run long: the essay, the wedding toast, the rule of life. A man from Najd once came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hair uncombed, voice carrying, and asked what Islam asks of him.
Five prayers in a day and a night, the Prophet said. The fast of Ramadan. Zakat, the giving.
Anything more? Not unless you choose it freely. The man turned to go and swore: by God, I'll add nothing to this, and take nothing away.
And the Prophet said: he has succeeded, if he is truthful.

teach.b: So, the debate. One view says: keep the core, and keep it well. The man's short list was enough, the Prophet said, if he was true to it.
In Islam the duties are called fard, obligatory, and nothing replaces them.

teach.h: NAFL: THE EXTRAS THAT DRAW NEAR.
teach.b: The other view comes from a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet reports from God: my servant draws near to me with nothing more beloved to me than the duties I have laid on him, and my servant keeps drawing near with voluntary deeds, nafl, until I love him.
Extra prayers, extra fasting, extra giving: the road closer. Some Muslims add prayers around the obligatory ones, or fast on days that aren't required. Let the two views answer each other.
The first: a short list you keep is worth more than a long one you won't.
The second: the core is the floor, not the ceiling; love wants to give more. Islamic teaching holds both. The obligatory comes first and is most beloved, and the voluntary is a gift on top.
That's the teaching: a core you never drop, and extras you choose freely.
Cutting a rule in half can work the same way. Keep the lines you'd swear to, no more and no less. Mark the rest as extras, for the days love asks for more.

how: Muslims distinguish the obligatory duties (fard), such as the five daily prayers, the Ramadan fast and zakat, from voluntary acts (nafl), such as extra prayers and fasts, which some add to draw closer to God.

games.q: what does “cut it in half” mean?
o: keeping the core you'd swear to, and trimming the rest
halving each thing so it takes half as long
splitting your practice time with a friend each day

games.q: the core and the extras: tap the pairs.
p: words the Prophet reports from God

s: in Islam, keeping only the obligatory duties counts for nothing
the Prophet said the man who kept them, no more and no less, would succeed if truthful.
a hadith qudsi says voluntary deeds keep drawing the servant nearer to God
the duties are most beloved, and voluntary deeds draw nearer still (Bukhari 6502).

games.q: your friend keeps only the basics of her faith, and keeps them faithfully. her sister calls it lazy. what's the strongest case for your friend?
o: the Prophet said the man who kept the basics, no more, no less, would succeed if truthful.
extras are useless; the hadith says God doesn't care about voluntary acts.
basics don't matter if your heart is good; skip whatever feels hard.
games.why: the man from Najd promised the obligatory, no more and no less, and was told he'd succeed if truthful. Her sister has a case too: voluntary deeds draw near.

practice: Look over yesterday's version and choose the lines you'd keep even in a bad week: that's your core, small enough to keep.

Now picture one hard day next week, name what would get in the way, and make a plan: if that happens, I still keep the core. The rest are extras, given freely. Sit with that plan for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Cut it in half: keep the core you'd swear to, and let the rest be freely chosen extras, the way Islam names fard and nafl.

orig.note: Arabic: an obligatory duty. Voluntary deeds are nafl (نفل).

carryVoice: Keep this one: half, the core kept no more and no less, the extras given freely. Day 1690, trimmed.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 46 (Talha ibn Ubaydullah: a man from Najd with unkempt hair asks about Islam; five prayers in a day and night, the fast of Ramadan, zakat; 'unless you do so voluntarily'; he swears to add nothing and take nothing away; 'he will succeed if he is truthful')

Sahih al-Bukhari 6502 (hadith qudsi: My servant draws not near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than the duties I have enjoined on him, and keeps drawing near with voluntary deeds until I love him)
